title: Template Deployment Options Matrix (Docker, Fly.io, Render, Kubernetes) vs Redwood Modes
content:
Goal
- Provide a single reference matrix for which deployment recipes we ship with template repos (or link from template README) and how each maps to Redwood deployment modes (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private).
- The intent is not to be exhaustive (Heroku, GCP Cloud Run, etc.). We need a small set that covers: local/dev, "I want it live today", and "I want to run this in my cluster".

Definitions (Redwood modes)
- Hosted API: customer app runs anywhere; calls Redwood hosted endpoint over the public internet.
- Dedicated: same as Hosted from the app perspective; endpoint is dedicated capacity; often additional network constraints, higher throughput expectations.
- Private (VPC / on-prem): customer app typically runs in same VPC or on-prem network; endpoint may not be reachable from public internet; customers frequently require explicit egress controls and private connectivity.

Assumptions / constraints
- Template apps are reference implementations; they should not imply Redwood endorses a specific PaaS for regulated workloads.
- Observability must work in all recipes: traces + metrics via OpenTelemetry with minimal user editing.
- Secrets handling: no keys in repo; use platform secret store or env vars; logs must redact.
- Keep vendor lock-in minimal: recipes should be optional and easy to delete.

What we are shipping in v1 (proposal)
- REQUIRED in template repo: Dockerfile + docker-compose for local dev (includes local OTel collector).
- OPTIONAL docs recipes: Fly.io + Kubernetes.
- Render: link-only initially (common request from startups, but varies a lot by org; we can provide “known-good” config once we stabilize).

Matrix (rows = deployment recipe)

Columns:
- Complexity: Low / Med / High (estimated user effort)
- Best for: common user intent
- Languages: Python, TypeScript (both should be supported unless noted)
- Redwood fit: Hosted / Dedicated / Private (Good / OK / Not recommended)
- Networking: notes on outbound connectivity to Redwood + inbound to app
- Secrets: recommended approach
- Observability: collector strategy + gotchas
- Operational notes: autoscaling, cold starts, timeouts, streaming

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Docker (single container) + docker-compose (local)
- Complexity: Low
- Best for: local dev, internal eval, reproducible baseline for support; also works for simple self-host on VM.
- Languages: Python ✅ / TypeScript ✅
- Redwood fit:
  - Hosted: Good
  - Dedicated: Good
  - Private: OK (depends on network reachability; good for testing in-corp if Docker allowed)
- Networking:
  - Outbound HTTPS to Redwood endpoint.
  - App inbound: local port (e.g., 3000/8000). Behind proxy: user-managed.
- Secrets:
  - .env file in local dev (gitignored). Production: env vars injected by runtime.
- Observability:
  - Local OTel collector via docker-compose (per PR-107).
  - Default exporters: console/logging exporter for dev; optional OTLP endpoint env var for pushing to customer backend.
  - Gotchas: users forget to start collector; we need “doctor” checks.
- Operational notes:
  - Streaming: generally stable locally; issues appear behind proxies/load balancers.
  - Recommendation: this is our “support baseline” for reproductions.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Fly.io (PaaS) recipe
- Complexity: Med
- Best for: "get it live" demos, small prod for startups, quick shareable URL.
- Languages: Python ✅ / TypeScript ✅ (via Docker deploy)
- Redwood fit:
  - Hosted: Good
  - Dedicated: Good
  - Private: Not recommended (Fly network model typically conflicts with private-only endpoints; can work via VPN in some cases but not a default recommendation)
- Networking:
  - Outbound to Redwood over internet.
  - Inbound: Fly-managed TLS + routing.
- Secrets:
  - fly secrets set … (document exact commands).
- Observability:
  - Option A: run OTel collector as sidecar process in same VM (lightweight) OR export directly to customer OTLP endpoint.
  - For v1: recommend direct OTLP export to user backend if available; otherwise keep basic logs.
  - Gotchas: users confuse Redwood Console vs their own tracing backend; we must be explicit.
- Operational notes:
  - Autoscaling: simple scale count; cost control guidance needed.
  - Streaming: can be impacted by edge proxies; advise timeouts + keepalive.
  - See: redwood-examples PR-290.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3) Render (PaaS) recipe
- Complexity: Med (but more “click-ops” variability)
- Best for: startups already on Render; quick deploy from GitHub.
- Languages: Python ✅ / TypeScript ✅ (Docker or native build)
- Redwood fit:
  - Hosted: Good
  - Dedicated: Good
  - Private: Not recommended (same reasons as Fly; additionally, enterprise private networking varies)
- Networking:
  - Outbound to Redwood over internet.
  - Inbound: Render-managed.
- Secrets:
  - Render environment groups / service env vars.
- Observability:
  - Mixed: some users will not have OTLP sink.
  - For v1: at minimum, structured logs + correlation/request-id fields; traces optional.
  - If we publish: provide OTLP export env vars + guidance for running a managed collector elsewhere.
- Operational notes:
  - Streaming: depends heavily on Render proxy behavior; risk of support tickets if we “bless” it.
  - Recommendation: link-only in v1 (no hard guarantee). Add once we have repeated internal success.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4) Kubernetes (k8s) recipe (Helm-lite manifests)
- Complexity: High
- Best for: platform teams, enterprise PoCs, production in cluster, Dedicated/Private evaluations.
- Languages: Python ✅ / TypeScript ✅ (containerized)
- Redwood fit:
  - Hosted: OK (works, but overkill)
  - Dedicated: Good
  - Private: Good (most aligned; can route to private endpoints, private DNS, tighter egress)
- Networking:
  - Outbound to Redwood over customer-controlled egress.
  - Inbound: ingress controller (nginx/alb/etc.). Must document streaming/websocket settings and timeouts.
- Secrets:
  - Kubernetes Secrets + external secret manager integration recommended (ExternalSecrets, etc.).
  - Never mount keys into logs; verify redaction.
- Observability:
  - Strongest option: deploy OTel collector in cluster; app exports OTLP to collector service.
  - Provide sample collector config (align with Observability Pack PR-158).
  - Gotchas: cardinality (don’t tag per-user), PII redaction processors.
- Operational notes:
  - Best place to show: HPA, resource requests/limits, graceful shutdown for streaming.
  - Recommend adding a “minimal prod” profile vs “full” profile.
  - See: redwood-examples PR-291.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary table (quick scan)

Recipe | Complexity | Hosted | Dedicated | Private | Observability maturity | Recommend ship in v1?
- Docker + compose (local): Low | Good | Good | OK | High (local collector included) | YES (required)
- Fly.io: Med | Good | Good | Not rec | Med | YES (docs recipe)
- Render: Med | Good | Good | Not rec | Low-Med | MAYBE (link-only)
- Kubernetes: High | OK | Good | Good | High | YES (docs recipe)

Key guidance to include in template READMEs (notes for Wei/Elliot)
- Hosted vs Dedicated: for template app, the code path is identical; only endpoint + capacity/SLA differs. Recipes should not imply Dedicated requires different deploy.
- Private: explicitly call out that PaaS recipes are usually not appropriate; recommend k8s or “run in VPC” (Docker on VM) depending on customer setup.
- Observability: explain 3 modes:
  1) local dev collector (compose)
  2) production: export to existing OTLP endpoint / vendor
  3) k8s: in-cluster collector
- Streaming: provide known-good settings and a troubleshooting note (proxy buffering, idle timeouts, chunked transfer).

Open questions / TODO
- Do we want a generic “Docker on VM” production recipe (systemd + caddy/nginx) for Private customers who are not k8s-native?
- If telemetry headers are opt-in (proxy issues), ensure deployment recipes mention how to disable/enable them.
- Decide what we can support via Support: we should label recipes as “reference configs” and define what is in/out of scope.

Changelog
- 2025-03-11: Marked Render as link-only; clarified Private stance for PaaS. Added explicit observability modes and streaming proxy notes.
- 2025-02-14: Initial draft matrix.
